title: Mönchengladbach to Eighth Avenue: the Wounded Body Made Whole
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Sickly Boy of the Rhineland

stops.name: Mönchengladbach, birth in a gymnast's house
stops.campa: Joseph Hubertus Pilates is born on the ninth of December in the weaving town of Mönchengladbach in the Rhine Province, second child of Heinrich Friedrich Pilates, a metalworker of Greek descent and a prize-winning gymnast of the local Turnverein, and of a mother who practices naturopathy, laying hands and herbs on the sick of the street where doctors will not go. The house holds two disciplines at once, the bar and the poultice, the body drilled and the body dosed, and the boy is born already the meeting-ground of both.
suggested_refs: The civil birth register of Mönchengladbach, 9 December 1883, confirming the disputed birth year
sources: Pérez Pont & Aparicio Romero, Joseph Pilates: A Man's Life (2013)

stops.name: Mönchengladbach, the sickly child
stops.campa: The boy who will remake the fitness of a century is himself, in these years, a wreck of a child. Rickets bows what strength his legs have; asthma closes his chest on the coal-smoke air of the Ruhr's edge; rheumatic fever comes and leaves his heart and joints marked. He watches the other boys run in the Marktplatz and cannot follow. His mother doses him with her tinctures; his father, home from the Turnhalle, looks at his son and says nothing, but the look is itself a kind of sentence: that this body must be rebuilt, or it will not survive.
suggested_refs: The condition-triad, asthma, rickets, rheumatic fever, as recorded in every biography descending from the family's own account
sources: Pérez Pont & Aparicio Romero, Joseph Pilates: A Man's Life (2013)

stops.name: Mönchengladbach, the stone and the blind eye
stops.campa: At five years old, playing in the street, a bully's stone catches him full in the left eye. The sight in it never returns; he will carry the blindness silently for the rest of his life, rarely spoken of, never used as an excuse. It is the first of the wounds the tradition counts against him: asthma, rickets, fever, and now half-blindness; the ledger of frailty the grown man's body will be built, deliberately, muscle by muscle, to answer and outlast.
suggested_refs: The permanent left-eye blindness, noted in every biographical account, that Pilates himself almost never mentioned
sources: Pérez Pont & Aparicio Romero, Joseph Pilates: A Man's Life (2013)

stops.name: The Turnhalle, the father's discipline
stops.campa: Heinrich Pilates takes his failing son into the gymnastic hall of the Mönchengladbach Turnverein, the same drilled system of rings, bars, and mass calisthenics that Turnvater Jahn set going across the German lands to harden a defeated people into a nation. The boy who cannot run learns to hang, to climb, to hold. He is slow and sickness dogs him still, but something in the discipline of counted repetition, breath timed to motion, answers something in him; he begins, very early, to believe that the body is not a fixed sentence but an argument that can be won.
suggested_refs: The Turnverein movement of Friedrich Ludwig Jahn, whose gymnastic system trains the boy Joseph
sources: Pérez Pont & Aparicio Romero, Joseph Pilates: A Man's Life (2013)

stops.name: Mönchengladbach: the ancient Greeks, the ideal body
stops.campa: In illustrated books of antiquity the boy finds the figures he will spend his life trying to become: Greek statuary, the discus-throwers and wrestlers of marble, bodies proportioned as if geometry and health were the same fact. He begins, the family recalls, to model his own training on this old ideal: symmetry over bulk, control over brute force, the whole frame answering to a single intelligence rather than a set of separate muscles. He studies anatomy plates beside the statues, laying one over the other in his mind, a discipline he will still be preaching seventy years later on Eighth Avenue.
suggested_refs: The classical Greek statuary, discus-throwers, wrestlers, that furnishes his lifelong physical ideal
sources: Pérez Pont & Aparicio Romero, Joseph Pilates: A Man's Life (2013)
pilatesencyclopedia.com, 'Joseph Pilates: The Man Behind The Method'

stops.name: Mönchengladbach, the boy who poses for the anatomy chart
stops.campa: By fourteen the rebuilding is done: the asthmatic, rachitic child of ten years before is now fit enough, muscled and proportioned enough, to be hired posing for anatomical wall-charts, the kind hung in German schoolrooms to teach children the named muscles of a healthy man. He becomes, quite literally, a diagram of what a ruined body can be made into, a fact he will repeat all his life as the first proof of his method, before the method even has its name.
suggested_refs: The anatomical wall-charts of German schoolrooms, for which the teenage Joseph modeled

stops.name: Germany: gymnast, diver, skier, boxer, wrestler
stops.campa: Through his later teens and twenties the young man refuses to specialize: he trains as a gymnast, dives, skis in the winters, boxes, wrestles, and studies what fragments of yoga and Eastern martial discipline reach the German gymnasiums of the day. Each discipline he treats as a different lens on the same problem, control of the whole body by the mind, rather than a separate sport to master and set aside. Circus troupes and traveling shows begin to hire him as a strongman and physical performer; the eye that cannot see is never once mentioned in the programs.
suggested_refs: The many-sport apprenticeship, gymnastics, diving, skiing, boxing, wrestling, that precedes any single named discipline
sources: Pérez Pont & Aparicio Romero, Joseph Pilates: A Man's Life (2013)

segments.name: The Ring and the Sawdust Ring, England

stops.name: The crossing to England
stops.campa: In 1912 Joseph Pilates leaves Germany for England, one more young athlete crossing the water in search of a stage for a body that has become, by will alone, remarkable. He carries no formal trade but the trades of the ring and the circus tent: boxer, wrestler, gymnast, professional physical specimen. England in these years is thick with music-hall strongmen and traveling shows, and a German with a build like carved stone and a talent for stillness finds work quickly.
suggested_refs: The 1912 emigration from Germany to England, the first of his two Atlantic-scaled departures

stops.name: Blackpool, the Living Greek Statue
stops.campa: On the Blackpool piers, in the traveling circuses of the Webb Brothers and others like them, Pilates performs an act billed as the Living Greek Statue: a sequence of held poses, marble stillness broken into marble stillness, that turns his boyhood study of antique sculpture into a paying trade. To the crowd it is spectacle; to Pilates, by his own later account, it is a study in breath and balance no different from what he will teach on a mat forty years on. The body that could not run at five now holds an audience's eye by holding perfectly still.
suggested_refs: The Living Greek Statue act, performed with English traveling circuses at Blackpool

stops.name: London, self-defense trainer at Scotland Yard
stops.campa: Between engagements as boxer and circus performer, Pilates is retained to teach self-defense at police training schools and to detectives at Scotland Yard, drilling officers of the law in the same jiu-jitsu and boxing his own father set him to as a child. It is work that trusts his hands more than his papers, a foreigner training the guardians of a foreign capital in how to take a man down without a weapon, and it fixes in him the conviction that fitness is not vanity but a plain, practical necessity of the working body.
suggested_refs: The Scotland Yard self-defense instruction, training English detectives in jiu-jitsu and boxing

stops.name: Blackpool: the outbreak of war, an enemy alien
stops.campa: War comes on the fourth of August; the next day, Pilates, a German national performing and training in Blackpool, is registered as an enemy alien under British wartime law, index number 14001, his surname first mis-recorded as Pilatus. Thirty years old, in the finest physical condition of his life, he is now, overnight, not an athlete but a security risk. Within weeks the round-up begins that will take him first to a temporary camp and then, for three and a half years, out of the world entirely.
suggested_refs: The August 1914 enemy-alien registration, index number 14001, that ends his English career

stops.name: Lancaster Castle, the first internment
stops.campa: Pilates is taken to the temporary internment camp at Lancaster Castle, one of thousands of German civilians swept off the streets of Britain in the war's first weeks. He will not fight in this war; he will instead spend it locked in stone, and the tradition holds that even here he cannot be idle; he sets fellow internees to wrestling and calisthenics in the castle yard, refusing the camp's first temptation, which is to let the body rot along with the months.
suggested_refs: Lancaster Castle, his first internment camp, roughly twelve months before transfer to the Isle of Man

stops.name: Knockaloe, Camp 4: the crossing to the Isle of Man
stops.campa: On the twelfth of September Pilates is transferred to Knockaloe, the vast internment camp above Peel on the Isle of Man, and lodged in Camp 4 among the more than twenty thousand German and Austrian men held there at the war's height. It is a city of huts and wire built for no other purpose than waiting; the internees name it, with the black humor of the caged, Kaiser's Rest. Pilates will not leave this ground for three and a half years, the longest single stretch of his life, and the crucible in which the method is actually forged.
suggested_refs: Knockaloe Camp above Peel, Isle of Man, the largest civilian internment camp of the war
sources: National Geographic, 'The exercise phenomenon born in a prisoner-of-war camp'

stops.name: Knockaloe, the library and the anatomy books
stops.campa: Camp 4 holds a library of several thousand volumes, gathered by internees who include doctors, scholars, and men of every trade the German diaspora in England once practiced; among them are texts of medicine, anatomy, and sport that Pilates reads and re-reads through the slow years of the camp. Here, between the wire and the drilling yard, the boy's old study of Greek statuary and the man's practical schooling in boxing and gymnastics begin to fuse into something closer to a system, not yet named, but already shaped by the discipline of having nothing to do but think about the body.
suggested_refs: The Camp 4 library at Knockaloe, stocked by the internees themselves with medical and anatomical texts
sources: National Geographic, 'The exercise phenomenon born in a prisoner-of-war camp'

stops.name: Knockaloe, the cats teach him to move
stops.campa: He watches the camp cats, half-starved like every other creature behind the wire, stretch themselves each morning before they hunt: long, unhurried extensions through the whole spine, never rushed, never wasted, and he sees in them exactly the economy of motion he has been hunting for in books. They are lithe and springy, he will say long afterward, terribly efficient as they aim for their prey, no strength spent that the moment does not need. He begins deliberately imitating the stretch of a starving cat, and the observation becomes, in his own telling, one root of everything that follows.
stops.quote: They were lithe and springy and terribly efficient as they aimed for their prey.
stops.quote_source: Robert Wernick, 'Learning to be an Animal,' Sports Illustrated, 12 February 1962
suggested_refs: The Knockaloe camp cats, cited by Pilates himself as an early model for economical movement
sources: yellowpilates.com, 'What Cats Taught Joseph Pilates at Knockaloe'

stops.name: Knockaloe, referee at the boxing ring
stops.campa: The camp's own newspaper, the Lager Zeitung, records in its January number Pilates refereeing bouts at the camp's boxing matches, one more entry in a camp life he organizes as fully as he can: gymnastic festivals, wrestling tournaments, physical instruction offered to any of the eight thousand men in his reach who will take it. A camp captain will later write of him as the tireless one, always willing, never idle in four and a half truly horrible years, a verdict rendered by men who had every reason to remember only the wire and the cold.
stops.quote: To our friend, Mr Pilates, professor and instructor of physical education, always willing... the most unselfish during four and a half truly horrible years.
stops.quote_source: Testimonial of a fellow internee, quoted in the Knockaloe camp record
suggested_refs: The Camp 4 Lager Zeitung, January 1917, recording Pilates as boxing referee and instructor

stops.name: Knockaloe hospital, the bedsprings and the invalids
stops.campa: Among men broken by wartime illness and the imprisonment itself, Pilates works in and around the camp hospital, and here he takes the springs from the iron hospital cots and rigs them to the bed frames, top and bottom, so that patients too weak to stand can still work against resistance lying down. It is the improvisation the whole trade will trace itself back to: the spring-and-frame logic of the Reformer and the Cadillac, invented not in a New York workshop but at the bedside of dying and disabled prisoners of a war he did not choose to fight.
stops.quote: There I met people who were invalids because of wartime illnesses and due to their imprisonment.
stops.quote_source: Later interview, recorded in Pérez Pont & Aparicio Romero, Joseph Pilates: A Man's Life (2013)
suggested_refs: The spring-rigged hospital cots at Knockaloe, direct ancestor of the Reformer and the Cadillac
sources: coffeeordie.com, 'The First Pilates Studio May Have Started Inside an Internment Camp'

stops.name: Knockaloe: the flu comes, and none of his men fall
stops.campa: In the autumn of 1918 the influenza that is emptying the trenches and the cities of Europe sweeps into the camp as well, and hundreds of Knockaloe's twenty-three thousand men fall sick. Pilates will claim ever after, and his students will repeat it as an article of faith, that of the thousands who kept his daily regimen not a single one came down with the sickness, that they ended the war in better shape than they began it, proof before there is a name for the method that discipline of breath and body is itself a kind of armor.
stops.quote: They ended the war in better shape than when it started, and when the great influenza epidemic came sweeping over all the countries that had fought in the war, not one of them came down with it.
stops.quote_source: Attributed statement, recorded in Robert Wernick, Sports Illustrated (1962), and repeated in studio oral history
suggested_refs: The 1918 influenza epidemic at Knockaloe, and Pilates' own claim that his students went untouched

stops.name: Knockaloe, release and repatriation
stops.campa: In mid-March, five months after the armistice, the last internees are released and repatriated; Pilates crosses back to Germany on the twenty-second, three and a half years after he was first taken up in Blackpool. He leaves Knockaloe with no diploma, no patent yet filed, and no name for what he has built, only a body kept, by his own iron discipline, in full working order through a war he spent entirely behind wire, and a set of improvised machines and observed principles that have no home yet but his own mind.
suggested_refs: The March 1919 release and repatriation of the Knockaloe internees to Germany

stops.name: Germany, home after four and a half years
stops.campa: Pilates returns to a defeated, revolutionary Germany, the Kaiser gone, the mark falling, the whole order his father's gymnastic generation served now in ruins. He is thirty-five, has spent four and a half years a prisoner of a war he never fired a shot in, and carries in his head a body of exercises tested on eight thousand starving men rather than in any university or clinic. He begins, quietly, to teach: private clients, athletes, anyone in the wrecked Weimar cities willing to pay a foreign-trained gymnast to put a ruined body back in order.
suggested_refs: Post-war Weimar Germany, the ruined economy in which Pilates first sets up as an independent trainer

stops.name: Hamburg: training the police, the Foot Corrector
stops.campa: In Hamburg, Pilates is engaged to train the city's military police in self-defense and physical conditioning, work that echoes his old Scotland Yard trade and pays enough to let him refine his private practice besides. This year he files his first patent, the Foot Corrector: a small spring-loaded device to rebuild the arch and the toes, the foot being, in his system, the first joint in a chain that runs unbroken to the skull. It is the first of what will become, over his lifetime, more than two dozen patented machines, and it is filed in Germany, years before Contrology has an American address.
suggested_refs: The Foot Corrector, 1922, Pilates' first patented apparatus, filed while training the Hamburg police

stops.name: Hamburg, Rudolf von Laban's dancers
stops.campa: Rudolf von Laban, the choreographer and theorist remaking European dance from his new Hamburg school, watches Pilates at work and takes note of his strengthening exercises, weaving elements of them into his own movement classes for dancers already schooled in Dalcroze's eurythmics and Bess Mensendieck's Körperkultur. It is the first crossing, in Pilates' own lifetime, of his discipline into the world of professional dance, a rehearsal, though neither man can know it, for the far larger crossing that will happen a decade later in a shared building on Eighth Avenue in New York.
suggested_refs: Rudolf von Laban's Hamburg dance school, 1923, the first documented crossing of Pilates' exercises into dance training
sources: yorkpilates.com, 'Creativity and Structure: Laban and Pilates'

stops.name: Hamburg: the new German army, and a refusal
stops.campa: Pilates' reputation as a trainer of soldiers and police reaches high enough that he is invited to bring his system to the training of the new German army being quietly rebuilt under Weimar's restrictions. He does not take the post. The political direction of the country unsettles him, and the invitation becomes, in the tradition his students later tell, the final push toward the decision he has been turning over for months: to leave Germany for America, and to build whatever he is building somewhere the state has no claim on it.
suggested_refs: The declined invitation to train the new German army, 1925, cited as the trigger for his emigration
sources: vitapilates.co.uk, 'A man ahead of his time'

segments.name: The Crossing and the Gymnasium on Eighth Avenue

stops.name: Hamburg harbor, the Westphalia sails
stops.campa: Pilates boards the S.S. Westphalia at Hamburg, forty-two years old, carrying little more than his notebooks, his patented Foot Corrector, and two and a half decades of self-taught physical philosophy, bound for a country he has never seen and a language he barely speaks. It is his second and final departure across water in search of ground to build on: the first, to England in 1912, ended in barbed wire; this one he means to make permanent.
suggested_refs: The S.S. Westphalia, the ship of Pilates' 1926 emigration from Hamburg to New York

stops.name: Mid-Atlantic, Clara Zeuner and the arthritic hands
stops.campa: On the crossing he meets Anna Clara Zeuner, forty-three, traveling to America to find work, her hands drawn and painful with arthritis. Pilates shows her a handful of exercises on the open deck; within days, the pain in her hands eases, and something more than gratitude passes between the German gymnast and the German schoolteacher going, separately, to the same unknown city. By the time the Westphalia makes landfall they have already decided, without a wedding and without a word to the shipping clerks, to build a life and a business together.
suggested_refs: Clara Zeuner, met aboard the Westphalia, whose arthritic hands were the first body Pilates treated in the New World

stops.name: New York Harbor, the immigrant arrives
stops.campa: The Westphalia docks and Joseph Pilates steps onto American ground with no English worth mentioning, no capital, and no credential but a body forty years in the perfecting and a head full of unnamed exercises. New York in 1926 is thick with boxers, wrestlers, vaudeville strongmen, and immigrant trainers of every description; he finds his way, as so many before him, to a shared floor of gymnasiums and rehearsal rooms where a man can rent space by the hour and see what a new country will pay for.
suggested_refs: The port of New York, April 1926, landfall of Pilates' permanent emigration

stops.name: 939 Eighth Avenue: a boxer's gymnasium, and the Universal Reformer
stops.campa: Pilates begins working out of a boxers' training gym at 939 Eighth Avenue, in a building that happens also to house several dance schools and rehearsal spaces, a coincidence of real estate that will remake his whole career. Here he files the American patent for what he names the Universal Reformer, the spring-and-carriage machine descended in a straight line from the rigged bedsprings of the Knockaloe hospital, and begins building the apparatus with his own hands for whichever boxers, dancers, and laborers will pay to use it.
suggested_refs: The Universal Reformer, patented after emigration, the direct descendant of the Knockaloe hospital bedsprings
sources: rhinebeckpilates.com, '939 8th Avenue and Other Original Studios'

stops.name: 939 Eighth Avenue, Joe and Clara take the lease
stops.campa: By the turn of the decade Joseph and Clara have taken over the gymnasium outright, the boxers' floor becoming what regulars start calling the Body Conditioning Gym. Clara, never his wife in law but always his wife in practice, keeps the books, calms the anxious, and teaches with a patience Joseph does not always have; students will say for decades after that she is the true teacher of the method even as his name is the one on the door. Between them a business is built on nothing but word of mouth and the visible, undeniable fact of restored bodies.
suggested_refs: The Body Conditioning Gym at 939 Eighth Avenue, run jointly by Joseph and Clara from 1930

stops.name: New York: the Wunda Chair, the apparatus multiplies
stops.campa: Pilates files the patent for the Wunda Chair, a low box of springs and a pedal that folds flat enough to double as ordinary furniture: apparatus disguised as domestic object, meant for clients too poor or too private to buy a full Reformer. It joins the Cadillac, or Trapeze Table, rigged with overhead bars for the bedridden and the newly injured, and the Ladder Barrel for the spine. Each machine still carries, underneath its varnish, the same logic first improvised on hospital cots on an island prison camp: spring resistance standing in for gravity the weak body cannot yet fight alone.
suggested_refs: The Wunda Chair, patented 1931/1934, and the growing family of Pilates apparatus

stops.name: New York, Your Health is published
stops.campa: Pilates publishes his first book, Your Health, laying out in his own broken, urgent English the argument he has been making with his hands for twenty years: that modern civilization, its chairs, its habits of shallow breath, its neglect of posture, is itself a disease, and that the cure is a disciplined, daily return to the body's own correct use. It is a slim, strange, evangelical little volume, more manifesto than manual, and it is the first time the system built in a Rhineland childhood and an Isle of Man prison camp appears in print under his own name.
suggested_refs: Your Health (1934), Joseph Pilates' first published book

stops.name: 939 Eighth Avenue, Eve Gentry begins
stops.campa: A young dancer named Eve Gentry begins studying under Joseph and Clara, the start of what will become one of the longest direct apprenticeships of any student who ever passed through the Eighth Avenue floor. She and the handful of dancers, boxers, and injured professionals who study seriously with Joe in these years are the first of what later generations will call the Elders, the living chain by which a method invented by one uncredentialed immigrant will, decades after his death, still be taught hand to hand rather than merely read from a book.
suggested_refs: Eve Gentry, one of the earliest and longest-studying of the first-generation Pilates Elders
sources: corevapilates.com, 'Pilates Elders: The First Generation of Teachers'

stops.name: 939 Eighth Avenue: Contrology, body, mind, and spirit
stops.campa: By now Pilates has a name for what he teaches: Contrology, the conscious mastery of the body by the mind, breath treated as the first exercise and the last. He drills his principle daily on the gym floor: that no motion is worth performing without full attention, that a hundred careless repetitions teach the body nothing a dozen exact ones cannot teach better. Breathing, he insists to every client who climbs onto the Reformer, is the first act of life and the last; a body that cannot breathe correctly cannot, in his system, be said to be alive correctly either.
stops.quote: Breathing is the first act of life and the last. Our very life depends on it.
stops.quote_source: Joseph H. Pilates, Return to Life Through Contrology (1945)
suggested_refs: 'Contrology,' Pilates' own name for his method, centered on breath and the mind's mastery of the body
sources: Joseph H. Pilates, Return to Life Through Contrology (1945)

stops.name: 939 Eighth Avenue, Balanchine sends his dancers
stops.campa: The choreographer George Balanchine, building in New York the company that will become the New York City Ballet, discovers the immigrant's gym among the dance studios and rehearsal floors of 939 Eighth Avenue and begins sending injured dancers to Joe and Clara for what today would be called rehabilitation; in 1941 the young Romana Kryzanowska, ankle chipped at the School of American Ballet, is delivered to the studio by Balanchine himself. He trains there too and calls it simply Joe's; within a few years the gym meant for pugilists is, without anyone planning it, the private clinic of American ballet.
suggested_refs: George Balanchine's referrals of injured dancers, Romana Kryzanowska's 1941 ankle among the first, to the Eighth Avenue gym
sources: pointemagazine.com, 'The Interconnected History of Pilates and Ballet'
kiralamb.com, 'Pilates & the Myth of the Dancer's Body'

stops.name: New York, Return to Life Through Contrology is published
stops.campa: With the journalist William John Miller, Pilates publishes Return to Life Through Contrology, the fuller statement of his system: thirty-four mat exercises set out in photographs of his own aging but still remarkable body, framed by his declarations on posture, breath, and the folly of modern civilization's neglect of its own physical machinery. It opens with the sentence that will outlive every apparatus he ever patented: that fitness is not vanity but the foundation of a happy life, and it becomes, in time, the founding scripture of a method practiced, a century later, by tens of millions who never once set foot on Eighth Avenue.
stops.quote: Physical fitness is the first requisite of happiness.
stops.quote_source: Joseph H. Pilates, Return to Life Through Contrology (1945), opening line
suggested_refs: Return to Life Through Contrology (1945), Pilates' definitive book and the mat-work canon of thirty-four exercises
sources: Joseph H. Pilates & William J. Miller, Return to Life Through Contrology (1945)

stops.name: 939 Eighth Avenue, Carola Trier, the refugee contortionist
stops.campa: Carola Trier, a dancer and contortionist who fled Nazi-occupied Europe with nothing, begins studying seriously with Joe in these years, one more body arriving at Eighth Avenue already marked by a war Pilates himself once sat out behind wire on a different island. She will become, within the decade, the first student he formally authorizes to open her own studio under his name, the method beginning, deliberately now, to propagate itself beyond the one floor where it was built.
suggested_refs: Carola Trier, refugee dancer and the first Pilates-authorized studio outside Eighth Avenue (1960)
sources: corevapilates.com, 'Pilates Elders: The First Generation of Teachers'

stops.name: 939 Eighth Avenue, Ron Fletcher, from Martha Graham's company
stops.campa: Ron Fletcher, a principal dancer with Martha Graham's company, comes to Joe's floor for the same reason Balanchine's dancers came a generation earlier, an injury the ballet's own doctors cannot fully mend, and stays to become one of the most fervent of the Elders, later carrying his own inflected version of the work to Los Angeles. Graham's studio and Balanchine's, rivals in nearly everything else, meet without contradiction on the mats of a single immigrant gymnasium on Eighth Avenue.
suggested_refs: Ron Fletcher, dancer with the Martha Graham company, later founder of Fletcher Work
sources: corevapilates.com, 'Pilates Elders: The First Generation of Teachers'

stops.name: 939 Eighth Avenue, Romana and Kathy, the last generation
stops.campa: Romana Kryzanowska, a former dancer who first studied under Joe as a teenager in the 1940s, returns in these years to work alongside him full-time, absorbing the exact sequences and corrections that she will, after his death, carry forward as the self-declared guardian of classical Contrology. Kathy Stanford Grant studies alongside her. Between them and Eve Gentry, Carola Trier, Ron Fletcher, Bruce King, Lolita San Miguel, Mary Bowen, and Jay Grimes, the whole living transmission of the method, never fully written down, no diploma ever issued, passes from one uncredentialed immigrant into a dozen pairs of hands.
suggested_refs: Romana Kryzanowska and Kathy Stanford Grant, among the last generation to study directly under Joseph and Clara
sources: corevapilates.com, 'Pilates Elders: The First Generation of Teachers'

stops.name: 939 Eighth Avenue, the old man's vigor
stops.campa: Sports Illustrated sends a writer to the gym and finds a septuagenarian smoking a cigar, bare-chested in winter, who challenges a photographer forty years his junior to an arm-wrestling match and wins it outright. Pilates never touches aspirin, he tells visitors, and has never once been injured in a life spent boxing, wrestling, and climbing on his own machines; the whole country, he says, ought to be doing his exercises, and would be happier for it. It is vanity, and it is also, by every visible measure, simply true.
stops.quote: I must be right. Never an aspirin. Never injured a day in my life. The whole country, the whole world, should be doing my exercises. They'd be happier.
stops.quote_source: Interview, 1965, widely recorded in Pilates studio historiography
suggested_refs: The Sports Illustrated profile of the early 1960s, and its account of the cigar-smoking, arm-wrestling old man

stops.name: 939 Eighth Avenue, we retire too early
stops.campa: In his eightieth year Pilates still teaches every day, and still preaches the doctrine of long, undiminished life that his own body appears to prove: that civilization has convinced people to grow old and useless decades before their bodies require it, that a properly kept spine and a properly used lung ought to carry a man in vigor into his tenth decade. He means it as science, not consolation, and points at himself, cigar in hand, spine still supple, climbing daily onto his own machines, as the demonstration.
stops.quote: We retire too early and we die too young, our prime of life should be in the 70's and old age should not come until we are almost 100.
stops.quote_source: Attributed remark to a reporter in his last years, canonical in Pilates studio tradition
suggested_refs: Pilates' own doctrine of delayed old age, embodied in his continuing to teach and train into his eighties
sources: Joseph H. Pilates, Return to Life Through Contrology (1945)

segments.name: The Fire and the Return to Life

stops.name: 939 Eighth Avenue, the fire in the storeroom
stops.campa: A fire breaks out in the storage room at the back of the studio floor, consuming decades of notebooks, photographs, and apparatus records that exist nowhere else. Pilates, eighty-six years old by his own count and still smoking his daily cigar, goes in after the smoke to see what can be saved, and in the wreckage his foot goes through a burned floorboard; he catches himself before the fall becomes worse, an old gymnast's reflex holding one more time. He carries the smoke out of the building in his lungs, where, his students will always afterward believe, it never fully leaves him.
suggested_refs: The January 1966 fire at 939 Eighth Avenue, in the tradition's account the origin of his final decline

stops.name: New York, the failing breath
stops.campa: Through the last year his breath, the very organ his whole system was built to master, begins visibly to fail him, the cigars of sixty years and the smoke of the fire converging, by every account, on the same ruined lungs. He teaches still, more slowly, correcting students from a chair when he can no longer stand over the Reformer himself, insisting to the end that the discipline itself has never once failed him, only the body's raw material finally giving out beneath a lifetime of use he never once regretted spending.
suggested_refs: Pilates' final year of teaching, physically diminished but still instructing at the studio
sources: Pérez Pont & Aparicio Romero, Joseph Pilates: A Man's Life (2013)

stops.name: New York, death in the city that made him famous
stops.campa: Joseph Pilates dies in New York on the ninth of October, of advanced emphysema, forty-one years after landing penniless at the port with nothing but a body and a set of unnamed exercises. He leaves no will and no line of legal succession: the empire of Contrology has no charter, no franchise, no single named heir; only Clara, and the dozen Elders who learned the work hand to hand on the Eighth Avenue floor, to carry a method that exists nowhere in writing exactly as it existed in him. In the hospital, near the end, he is remembered saying the sentence his whole life had been an argument for.
stops.quote: I'm fifty years ahead of my time!
stops.quote_source: Reported deathbed remark, recorded in Pilates studio oral history and cited in retrospectives on the 50th anniversary of his death
suggested_refs: The New York Times obituary describing him at the last as still limber, still upright, a white-maned old lion of a man
sources: fitnessmarkt.com, 'On the 50th anniversary of his death'

stops.name: Ferncliff Cemetery, Hartsdale: burial
stops.campa: He is buried at Ferncliff Cemetery north of the city, among the actors and musicians and the merely rich of a country that gave the sickly Rhineland boy his second life. Clara keeps the studio on Eighth Avenue running three more years before she too steps back, dying in 1977; by then Romana Kryzanowska and the other Elders have already begun carrying Contrology out of one gymnasium and into a hundred, a thousand, a method with no trademark that will hold, no single school that can claim the whole of it, exactly, in its way, as ungovernable and as durable as the man who built it out of springs and a starved cat's stretch.
